pos: adj. (destructive; having the quality of killing or ruining, often slowly and without alarm)
etymology: Latin perniciosus, from per-, thoroughly, and nex, death. The AV uses it once, of the ways false teachers make popular (2Pe 2:2).
biblical_def: Pernicious means quietly destructive. Peter's use is of doctrine that spreads: false teachers “shall bring in damnable heresies, even denying the Lord that bought them… and many shall follow their pernicious ways; by reason of whom the way of truth shall be evil spoken of” (2Pe 2:1–2). Paul warns the Ephesian elders that “grievous wolves” shall enter in, not sparing the flock, and that some shall arise from among their own selves (Act 20:29–30). The Lord notes the disguise: false prophets come “in sheep's clothing, but inwardly they are ravening wolves” (Mat 7:15). And the spread is like disease: “their word will eat as doth a canker” (2Ti 2:17).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines pernicious as destructive; having the quality of killing, destroying or injuring; very injurious or mischievous.
webster_full: PERNICIOUS, a. Destructive; having the quality of killing, destroying or injuring; very injurious or mischievous.
Sin is pernicious to the soul, as well as to the body.
2. Quick. [Not in use.]
PERNICIOUSLY, adv. Destructively; with ruinous tendency.
scriptures: But there were false prophets also among the people, even as there shall be false teachers among you, who privily shall bring in damnable heresies, even denying the Lord that bought them, and bring upon themselves swift destruction.
And many shall follow their pernicious ways; by reason of whom the way of truth shall be evil spoken of.
For I know this, that after my departing shall grievous wolves enter in among you, not sparing the flock.
Mat 7:15
Beware of false prophets, which come to you in sheep's clothing, but inwardly they are ravening wolves.
And their word will eat as doth a canker: of whom is Hymenaeus and Philetus;
corruption_summary: Error is expected to arrive looking dangerous, and the pernicious kind arrives looking attractive and popular.
corruption_paragraphs: Second Peter 2:2 contains a detail that ought to be read aloud in every discussion of doctrinal drift: many shall follow their pernicious ways. Not a fringe, not a handful — many. Ruinous teaching does not survive by being obviously ruinous; it survives by being appealing, and the size of the following is no evidence at all about its soundness. A church that measures a ministry by its growth has adopted the one metric this verse explicitly refuses.

Acts 20:30 supplies the harder half of the warning. Paul tells the Ephesian elders that grievous wolves will come in from outside, and then says also of your own selves shall men arise, speaking perverse things, to draw away disciples after them. The danger is not only external. It comes from the eldership, from men the congregation trusts, and the motive named is the drawing away of disciples after them — a following of one's own. That is why the discipline of watching doctrine cannot be delegated entirely to the men being watched.

Second Timothy 2:17 gives the pathology in one image: their word will eat as doth a canker — a gangrene, spreading through living tissue, painless at the edge. That is the difference between a heresy and a pernicious teaching. A frontal denial of the resurrection provokes resistance; a slow reweighting of emphases, a doctrine quietly dropped from the preaching, a category of sin no longer named, meets none. The remedy Paul prescribes in the same chapter is unspectacular: a workman rightly dividing the word of truth, and a man who departs from iniquity.
roots_summary: Greek apoleia (G684), destruction, perdition; hairesis (G139), heresy, a chosen party; lukos barus (G3074), grievous wolf; gaggraina (G1044), a canker, gangrene.
roots_lines: Greek apoleia (G684) — destruction; 2 Peter 2:1–3, Philippians 3:19, Matthew 7:13 — rendered both damnable and pernicious in 2 Peter 2.
Greek hairesis (G139) — heresy; 2 Peter 2:1, Galatians 5:20, Titus 3:10.
Greek gaggraina (G1044) — gangrene, canker; 2 Timothy 2:17 only.
usage: “Many shall follow their pernicious ways” — many, and that is the point.
“Of your own selves shall men arise” — said to an eldership.
“Their word will eat as doth a canker” — painless at the edge.

pos: v. and adj. (to fall away from the qualities of one's kind; grown worse than the stock one came from)
etymology: Latin degenerare, from de-, down from, and genus, race or kind — to fall away from one's kind. Jeremiah's vine is the governing figure.
biblical_def: To degenerate is to fall away from what one's kind should be. Jeremiah's figure is exact: “Yet I had planted thee a noble vine, wholly a right seed: how then art thou turned into the degenerate plant of a strange vine unto me?” (Jer 2:21). Isaiah puts it in metal: “Thy silver is become dross, thy wine mixed with water” (Isa 1:22). The Lord charges a working, patient, orthodox church with it: “Nevertheless I have somewhat against thee, because thou hast left thy first love” (Rev 2:4). Paul asks the Galatians the direct question: “Having begun in the Spirit, are ye now made perfect by the flesh?” (Gal 3:3). And Hosea names the worst feature: “gray hairs are here and there upon him, yet he knoweth not” (Hos 7:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines degenerate as to fall from a perfect or good state into a less excellent or worse state; to become of a lower type than the parent stock.
webster_full: DEGENERATE, v.i. To become of a lower type; to fall from a perfect or good state into a less excellent or worse state; to be or grow worse.
DEGENERATE, a. Having fallen from a perfect or good state into a less excellent or worse state; having lost something of the good qualities possessed; having declined in natural or moral worth.
scriptures: Jer 2:21
Yet I had planted thee a noble vine, wholly a right seed: how then art thou turned into the degenerate plant of a strange vine unto me?
Isa 1:22
Thy silver is become dross, thy wine mixed with water:
Rev 2:4
Nevertheless I have somewhat against thee, because thou hast left thy first love.
Gal 3:3
Are ye so foolish? having begun in the Spirit, are ye now made perfect by the flesh?
Hos 7:9
Strangers have devoured his strength, and he knoweth it not: yea, gray hairs are here and there upon him, yet he knoweth not.
corruption_summary: Decline is expected to announce itself, and the Bible's picture is of a man who does not know it has happened.
corruption_paragraphs: Hosea 7:9 is the most unnerving verse on the subject and it takes two clauses. Strangers have devoured his strength, and he knoweth it not; gray hairs are here and there upon him, yet he knoweth not. The repetition is the message. Degeneration is not experienced from the inside as a fall; it is experienced as normal, because the standard degrades along with the thing being measured. A church does not usually feel itself growing cold. It feels itself being reasonable, and only an outside measure — Scripture, or an older saint, or a comparison with what it once was — can register the change.

Revelation 2 is the case study, and its details should end any complacency built on activity. The Ephesian church had works, labour, patience, could not bear evil men, had tried false apostles and found them liars, had borne and not fainted. By every visible metric it was the soundest church on the list — and the Lord says I have somewhat against thee, because thou hast left thy first love, and threatens to remove its candlestick. Doctrinal vigilance and hard work had continued after the love that produced them had gone, which is exactly how degeneration hides.

The remedy given in Revelation 2:5 is worth noting for its shape: remember, repent, and do the first works. It begins with memory, because a man who does not know he has declined cannot repent of it, and it ends with action rather than feeling — do the first works. Jeremiah 2:21 says the same thing about origin: God planted a noble vine, wholly a right seed, and the strange vine is a departure from what was given rather than a failure to achieve something new. Recovery in Scripture is nearly always a return.
roots_summary: Hebrew sur (H5494), degenerate, turned aside; sig (H5509), dross; Greek enarchomai / epiteleo (G1728, G2005), to begin / to complete; aphiemi (G863), to leave, let go.
roots_lines: Hebrew surey haggephen (H5494) — the degenerate shoots of the vine; Jeremiah 2:21 only.
Hebrew sig (H5509) — dross; Isaiah 1:22, 1:25, Psalm 119:119, Proverbs 25:4.
Greek aphekas (G863) — thou hast left; Revelation 2:4 — left, not lost.
usage: “Gray hairs are here and there upon him, yet he knoweth not” — twice, he knoweth not.
“Thou hast left thy first love” — said to the busiest church on the list.
“Remember… repent, and do the first works” — memory first, then action.

pos: adj. (feigned; invented; not real, though presented as real)
etymology: Latin fictitius, from fingere, to shape or feign — the same root as fiction and figment. Calvin's regular charge against invented worship is that it offers God a fictitious deity of the mind's own making.
biblical_def: A fictitious thing is invented and passed off as real. Peter draws the contrast with his own testimony: “we have not followed cunningly devised fables, when we made known unto you the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, but were eyewitnesses of his majesty” (2Pe 1:16). Paul tells Timothy to “refuse profane and old wives' fables” (1Ti 4:7), warns of those who “shall turn away their ears from the truth, and shall be turned unto fables” (2Ti 4:4), and of “Jewish fables, and commandments of men, that turn from the truth” (Tit 1:14). Jeremiah names the source of invented revelation: “they speak a vision of their own heart, and not out of the mouth of the LORD” (Jer 23:16).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines fictitious as feigned; imaginary; not real; counterfeit; false; not genuine; as fictitious fame, or a fictitious story.
webster_full: FICTITIOUS, a. Feigned; imaginary; not real.
2. Counterfeit; false; not genuine; as fictitious fame.
FICTION, n. The act of feigning, inventing or imagining; as, by the mere fiction of the mind.
2. That which is feigned, invented or imagined.
scriptures: For we have not followed cunningly devised fables, when we made known unto you the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, but were eyewitnesses of his majesty.
But refuse profane and old wives' fables, and exercise thyself rather unto godliness.
And they shall turn away their ears from the truth, and shall be turned unto fables.
Tit 1:14
Not giving heed to Jewish fables, and commandments of men, that turn from the truth.
Thus saith the LORD of hosts, Hearken not unto the words of the prophets that prophesy unto you: they make you vain: they speak a vision of their own heart, and not out of the mouth of the LORD.
corruption_summary: A God is assembled from preference and called the God of the Bible, and the mind's workshop never runs out of material.
corruption_paragraphs: Calvin's phrase is that the human heart is a perpetual forge of idols, and the relevant point is that the forge works with religious material. Nobody sets out to worship a fiction. What happens is a slow assembly: attributes that comfort are kept, attributes that unsettle are quietly retired, and after some years a man is praying to a being of his own construction who agrees with him about everything. Jeremiah 23:16 describes the same manufacture in the prophets — a vision of their own heart, and not out of the mouth of the LORD — and the tell in that chapter is that such preaching says peace to those who despise God.

The remedy is the one Peter reaches for. Against the charge that the apostolic message was a cunningly devised fable he does not argue that it is edifying or that it works; he says we were eyewitnesses of his majesty, names the mountain, quotes the voice, and then adds that we have a more sure word of prophecy in the Scriptures. Christianity's defence against the charge of fiction has always been historical and textual rather than experiential, because an experience can be manufactured and an empty tomb cannot.

Second Timothy 4:4 describes the exchange with a passive and an active verb: they shall turn away their ears from the truth, and shall be turned unto fables. The first is a choice, the second is what happens next, and the order is fixed. Nobody adopts a fiction while the truth is still being heard; the fable moves in after the ear has been closed. Which is why Paul's instruction in the preceding verse is not a strategy for making truth competitive but simply preach the word; be instant in season, out of season.
roots_summary: Greek muthos (G3454), a fable, myth; sesophismenos (G4679), cunningly devised; plastos (G4112), moulded, feigned; Hebrew chazon libbam (H2377), a vision of their own heart.
roots_lines: Greek muthos (G3454) — fable, myth; 2 Peter 1:16, 1 Timothy 1:4, 4:7, 2 Timothy 4:4, Titus 1:14 — all five occurrences.
Greek sesophismenois muthois (G4679) — cunningly devised fables; 2 Peter 1:16.
Greek plastos (G4112) — feigned, moulded; 2 Peter 2:3 only.
usage: “Not… cunningly devised fables… but were eyewitnesses” — the defence is historical.
“A vision of their own heart” — the forge, working with religious material.
“Turn away their ears… and shall be turned unto fables” — the order is fixed.

pos: n. (craft; artifice; fineness of contrivance used to deceive — the AV spells it subtilty)
etymology: Latin subtilis, finely woven, from sub tela, under the loom's warp — a thread so fine it is not seen. The serpent's quality in Genesis 3:1 is the first thing said about him.
biblical_def: Subtlety is craft too fine to be noticed. It is the serpent's first attribute: “Now the serpent was more subtil than any beast of the field which the LORD God had made” (Gen 3:1). Paul fears its repetition: “I fear, lest by any means, as the serpent beguiled Eve through his subtilty, so your minds should be corrupted from the simplicity that is in Christ” (2Co 11:3). He names it in a man to his face: “O full of all subtilty and all mischief, thou child of the devil” (Act 13:10). The armour is given against it: “that ye may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil” (Eph 6:11). And forewarning is the defence: “we are not ignorant of his devices” (2Co 2:11).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines subtlety as craftiness; cunning; artifice; and refinement; extreme acuteness, as the subtlety of an argument.
webster_full: SUBTLETY, n. Thinness; fineness; exility; as the subtlety of air.
2. Refinement; extreme acuteness; as the subtlety of an argument or distinction.
3. Cunning; artifice; craftiness; guile.
SUBTILE, a. Thin; not dense or gross; sly in design; artful; cunning; insinuating.
scriptures: Gen 3:1
Now the serpent was more subtil than any beast of the field which the LORD God had made. And he said unto the woman, Yea, hath God said, Ye shall not eat of every tree of the garden?
But I fear, lest by any means, as the serpent beguiled Eve through his subtilty, so your minds should be corrupted from the simplicity that is in Christ.
And said, O full of all subtilty and all mischief, thou child of the devil, thou enemy of all righteousness, wilt thou not cease to pervert the right ways of the Lord?
Eph 6:11
Put on the whole armour of God, that ye may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil.
Lest Satan should get an advantage of us: for we are not ignorant of his devices.
corruption_summary: Temptation is expected to contradict Scripture, and the serpent's method was to quote it slightly wrong.
corruption_paragraphs: Genesis 3 repays close reading because nothing in it is a frontal attack. The serpent opens with a question and a misquotation just wide of the mark — Yea, hath God said, Ye shall not eat of every tree of the garden? — which is not what God said, and which invites Eve to correct him and so to take up the position of adjudicating the command. Her reply adds a prohibition God never gave (neither shall ye touch it), and the ground has already shifted before any denial is offered. Only then comes ye shall not surely die, and by that point it lands on prepared soil.

Second Corinthians 11:3 tells us what the target is, and it is not doctrine in the first instance: your minds should be corrupted from the simplicity that is in Christ. The word is singleness — an undivided attachment. Subtlety works by complication: adding a consideration, introducing a nuance, making a plain duty look naive, until a believer who could once have told you in a sentence what he owed his Lord now has a paragraph of qualifications. The corruption is of simplicity, and that is why it is so hard to see as loss; it feels like sophistication.

The defence Scripture gives is not cleverness. Second Corinthians 2:11 says we are not ignorant of his devices — the methods are documented, they are old, and they are in the Book. Ephesians 6 gives armour that is almost entirely defensive and entirely borrowed: truth, righteousness, the gospel of peace, faith, salvation, and one offensive weapon which is the word of God. That is exactly the weapon the Lord used in His own wilderness, against a tempter who by then had learnt to quote Scripture himself, and the difference was that He knew what the rest of the verse said.
roots_summary: Hebrew arum (H6175), subtil, crafty, prudent; Greek panourgia (G3834), craftiness; methodeia (G3180), wiles, methods; noema (G3540), device, thought.
roots_lines: Hebrew arum (H6175) — subtil, crafty; Genesis 3:1 — the same word is rendered prudent in Proverbs 12:16, 14:15.
Greek panourgia (G3834) — craftiness; 2 Corinthians 11:3, 4:2, Ephesians 4:14, Luke 20:23.
Greek methodeia (G3180) — wiles, scheming methods; Ephesians 6:11, 4:14 — both occurrences.
usage: “Yea, hath God said…?” — a question, and a misquotation just wide of the mark.
“Corrupted from the simplicity that is in Christ” — simplicity is the target.
“We are not ignorant of his devices” — they are documented, and old.

pos: n. and v. (an evasion of the point by a turn of words; a distinction raised to escape an obligation)
etymology: Probably from Latin quibus, the ablative plural of qui, common in legal documents — the lawyer's word made into a name for lawyerly evasion.
biblical_def: A quibble evades a duty by a technicality. The Lord's example is Corban: a man says of what would have relieved his parents, “It is a gift, by whatsoever thou mightest be profited by me”, and by that formula “ye suffer him no more to do ought for his father or his mother; making the word of God of none effect through your tradition” (Mar 7:11–13; Mat 15:5–6). He exposes the oath-distinctions the same way: “Whosoever shall swear by the temple, it is nothing; but whosoever shall swear by the gold of the temple, he is a debtor” (Mat 23:16). His remedy is to abolish the machinery: “let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil” (Mat 5:37).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines quibble as a turn of language to evade the point in debate; a start or turn from the point in question, or from plain truth; an evasion; a cavil.
webster_full: QUIBBLE, n. A turn of language to evade the point in debate; a start or turn from the point in question, or from plain truth; an evasion; a cavil.
Quirks or quibbles have no place in the search after truth.
2. A pun; a low conceit.
QUIBBLE, v.i. To evade the point in question by artifice, play upon words, or any conceit.
scriptures: Mar 7:11
But ye say, If a man shall say to his father or mother, It is Corban, that is to say, a gift, by whatsoever thou mightest be profited by me; he shall be free.
Mat 15:5
But ye say, Whosoever shall say to his father or his mother, It is a gift, by whatsoever thou mightest be profited by me;
Woe unto you, ye blind guides, which say, Whosoever shall swear by the temple, it is nothing; but whosoever shall swear by the gold of the temple, he is a debtor!
Mat 5:37
But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil.
Mar 7:13
Making the word of God of none effect through your tradition, which ye have delivered: and many such like things do ye.
corruption_summary: The letter is used against the law's own purpose, and the man who does it can usually cite chapter and verse.
corruption_paragraphs: Corban is the model and its horror is that it was religiously respectable. A man declares his property dedicated to God, which is a pious act; the consequence is that his aged parents cannot be helped from it, which is a violation of the Fifth Commandment; and the tradition upheld the dedication over the commandment. The Lord's verdict is that they made the word of God of none effect through their tradition — not by contradicting it but by constructing a lawful route around it. Nothing in the procedure was illegal. That is what makes it a quibble rather than a sin of defiance.

The oath-distinctions in Matthew 23 show the same machinery in miniature and reveal what drives it. Swearing by the temple does not bind; swearing by the gold of the temple does. The Lord's reply cuts underneath: whether is greater, the gold, or the temple that sanctifieth the gold? The system was engineered so that a man could produce an oath that sounded binding and was not, and the elaboration existed precisely so that the escape hatch would remain available. Complexity in a moral system is worth watching, because it is very often load-bearing.

Matthew 5:37 is the remedy and it is characteristically radical: dismantle the apparatus. Let your communication be Yea, yea; Nay, nay — a man whose plain word is reliable has no use for grades of oath, and the grades exist only where the plain word is not. The test to put to any of our own careful distinctions is the one the Lord applied: does this construction end by relieving me of a duty I would otherwise owe? If it does, the distinction is a quibble however sound the reasoning, and the reasoning is usually excellent.
roots_summary: Greek korban (G2878), a gift dedicated to God; akuroo (G208), to make of none effect; paradosis (G3862), tradition; opheilo (G3784), to be a debtor, be bound.
roots_lines: Greek korban (G2878) — a gift devoted to God; Mark 7:11 only; the Greek doron in Matthew 15:5.
Greek akuroo (G208) — to annul, make of none effect; Mark 7:13, Matthew 15:6, Galatians 3:17.
Greek opheiletes / opheilo (G3781, G3784) — debtor, bound; Matthew 23:16, 23:18.
usage: “Making the word of God of none effect through your tradition” — and nothing was illegal.
“Whether is greater, the gold, or the temple?” — the question that cuts underneath.
“Yea, yea; Nay, nay” — dismantle the apparatus.

pos: adj. (added from without; not belonging to a thing's own nature)
etymology: Latin adventitius, coming from abroad, from advenire, to arrive. The theological use is precise: sin is adventitious to human nature — it arrived, and was not part of what God made.
biblical_def: Something adventitious is added from outside and not native to the thing. The Reformed hold sin to be adventitious to human nature: God “saw every thing that he had made, and, behold, it was very good” (Gen 1:31); “God hath made man upright; but they have sought out many inventions” (Ecc 7:29); and sin arrived at a datable point, for “by one man sin entered into the world” (Rom 5:12). The parable gives the picture: “while men slept, his enemy came and sowed tares among the wheat” (Mat 13:25). And because the corruption was added, it can be removed without abolishing the man: “as in Adam all die, even so in Christ shall all be made alive” (1Co 15:22).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines adventitious as added extrinsically; accidental; not essentially inherent; foreign; something that does not belong to the nature of the thing.
webster_full: ADVENTITIOUS, a. Added extrinsically; accidental; not essentially inherent; casual; foreign.
Diseases of continuance get an adventitious strength from custom.
ADVENTITIOUSLY, adv. Accidentally.
scriptures: Gen 1:31
And God saw every thing that he had made, and, behold, it was very good. And the evening and the morning were the sixth day.
Ecc 7:29
Lo, this only have I found, that God hath made man upright; but they have sought out many inventions.
Rom 5:12
Wherefore, as by one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin; and so death passed upon all men, for that all have sinned:
But while men slept, his enemy came and sowed tares among the wheat, and went his way.
For as in Adam all die, even so in Christ shall all be made alive.
corruption_summary: Sin is treated as part of what it means to be human, which makes salvation a change of species rather than a cure.
corruption_paragraphs: The word looks technical and carries one of the load-bearing distinctions in Christian anthropology. If sin belongs to human nature as such, then to be saved is to stop being human, the incarnation is impossible (since Christ was truly man and without sin), and the resurrection body would be a different kind of thing from what we are. If sin is adventitious — a corruption that arrived and infected a good nature — then Christ can be fully man and sinless, salvation is restoration rather than replacement, and the glorified saint is more human than he is now, not less.

Ecclesiastes 7:29 states it with an economy nothing has improved on: God hath made man upright, but they have sought out many inventions. Two clauses, and everything is in them. The making is God's and it was upright; the inventions are ours and they came after. Total depravity, properly stated, is a claim about the extent of the corruption — every faculty touched — and not about its origin. The Reformed have never taught that God made a sinful thing, and the difference matters when a believer starts to despise his own body, appetites or reason as though they were the problem.

The parable of the tares adds the detail that explains the delay. The enemy sowed while men slept, and the servants ask whether to gather the tares up. The householder says no, lest ye root up also the wheat with them — let both grow together until the harvest. The corruption is genuinely foreign and will genuinely be removed, and it is not removed instantly, because the removal is bound up with a field the owner intends to keep. That is a doctrine of patience, and it is addressed to servants who would rather weed now.
roots_summary: Hebrew tob meod (H2896), very good; yashar (H3477), upright; Greek eiserchomai (G1525), to enter in; zizanion (G2215), tares, darnel.
roots_lines: Hebrew yashar (H3477) — upright, straight; Ecclesiastes 7:29, Deuteronomy 32:4.
Greek eiselthen (G1525) — entered in; Romans 5:12 — sin came in, it was not there.
Greek zizanion (G2215) — tares, darnel; Matthew 13:25–40 — a weed that looks like wheat until harvest.
usage: “God hath made man upright” — the making is His; the inventions are ours.
“By one man sin entered into the world” — entered, at a datable point.
“His enemy came and sowed tares” — foreign seed, in a field he means to keep.

pos: n. (defect; want of completeness; the incompleteness of the believer's holiness in this life)
etymology: Latin imperfectio, from in-, not, and perficere, to finish. The theological question is not whether a Christian is imperfect but what he is to do about knowing it.
biblical_def: Imperfection is the believer's present condition. Knowledge is partial: “we know in part, and we prophesy in part. But when that which is perfect is come, then that which is in part shall be done away” (1Co 13:9–10). Obedience is partial: “the good that I would I do not: but the evil which I would not, that I do” (Rom 7:19). Speech especially: “in many things we offend all. If any man offend not in word, the same is a perfect man” (Jas 3:2). Denial is self-deception: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1Jn 1:8). And the mature man's own account is Paul's: “Not as though I had already attained, either were already perfect: but I follow after” (Php 3:12).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines imperfection as defect; want of a part or of completeness; failure; fault; and, in morals, moral failing or defect.
webster_full: IMPERFECTION, n. Defect; fault; the want of perfection; as the imperfections of nature.
2. Failure; deficiency; incompleteness.
IMPERFECT, a. Not perfect; not complete in all its parts; defective.
2. Not fully formed.
scriptures: For we know in part, and we prophesy in part.
Rom 7:19
For the good that I would I do not: but the evil which I would not, that I do.
Jas 3:2
For in many things we offend all. If any man offend not in word, the same is a perfect man, and able also to bridle the whole body.
If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.
Php 3:12
Not as though I had already attained, either were already perfect: but I follow after, if that I may apprehend that for which also I am apprehended of Christ Jesus.
corruption_summary: Imperfection is used as an excuse to stop striving, or denied so that a man cannot admit what everyone can see.
corruption_paragraphs: The first misuse turns a diagnosis into a permission. Nobody's perfect is offered as the end of a conversation about a sin, and it functions as an amnesty. But Paul's own statement in Philippians 3:12 does not stop at the admission; the sentence continues — not as though I had already attained, but I follow after, if that I may apprehend that for which also I am apprehended of Christ Jesus — and the next verses use the language of an athlete straining forward. The knowledge of imperfection in Scripture always produces pursuit, never permission.

The second misuse is perfectionism, and its cruelty is that it forces sincere people to lie. If a believer must claim victory over conscious sin, then either he redefines sin downward until his record clears, or he conceals what he cannot deny, and both destroy the confession by which sin is dealt with. First John 1:8 is written into a letter about walking in the light and is followed immediately by verse 9 — if we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us. The admission is the doorway; a doctrine that closes it has closed the way to cleansing in the name of holiness.

James 3:2 aims at the place where imperfection is most visible and least often owned: in many things we offend all, and the test case is the tongue. A man may hold a clean external record for decades and still be undone by what he says in his own house, which is why the epistle spends a chapter on it. The doctrine is finally a hopeful one, because it is stated in the same breath as its terminus — when that which is perfect is come, that which is in part shall be done away. The imperfection is real, it is not permanent, and it is not the last thing said about the believer.
roots_summary: Greek ek merous (G3313), in part; teleios (G5046), perfect, complete, mature; ptaio (G4417), to stumble, offend; dioko (G1377), to pursue, follow after.
roots_lines: Greek ek merous (G3313) — in part; 1 Corinthians 13:9–12.
Greek teleios (G5046) — complete, mature, perfect; Philippians 3:12, 3:15, James 3:2, Matthew 5:48.
Greek dioko (G1377) — to pursue; Philippians 3:12–14, 1 Timothy 6:11, Hebrews 12:14.
usage: “Not as though I had already attained… but I follow after” — the sentence continues.
“In many things we offend all” — and the test case is the tongue.
“If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves” — and verse 9 follows.

pos: adj. (not to be broken, profaned or set aside)
etymology: Latin inviolabilis, from violare, to injure or profane. Applied in theology to the Scriptures, to God's oath, and to the covenant He has sworn.
biblical_def: What is inviolable cannot be broken. The Lord says it of Scripture in the middle of an argument that turns on a single word: “the scripture cannot be broken” (John 10:35). He says it of the law's smallest strokes: “Till heaven and earth pass, one jot or one tittle shall in no wise pass from the law, till all be fulfilled” (Mat 5:18). Balaam says it of God's word: “God is not a man, that he should lie; neither the son of man, that he should repent: hath he said, and shall he not do it?” (Num 23:19). Hebrews says it of the oath: “it was impossible for God to lie” (Heb 6:18). And God says it of the covenant: “My covenant will I not break, nor alter the thing that is gone out of my lips” (Psa 89:34).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines inviolable as not to be profaned; that ought not to be injured or treated with irreverence; not to be broken; as an inviolable oath, promise or vow.
webster_full: INVIOLABLE, a. Not to be profaned; that ought not to be injured or treated with irreverence, or made the subject of trespass; as an inviolable sanctuary.
2. Not to be broken; as an inviolable league, promise, vow or contract.
3. Not susceptible of hurt or wound; as inviolable saints.
INVIOLABLY, adv. Without failure of observance; without breach.
scriptures: John 10:35
If he called them gods, unto whom the word of God came, and the scripture cannot be broken;
Mat 5:18
For verily I say unto you, Till heaven and earth pass, one jot or one tittle shall in no wise pass from the law, till all be fulfilled.
God is not a man, that he should lie; neither the son of man, that he should repent: hath he said, and shall he not do it? or hath he spoken, and shall he not make it good?
Heb 6:18
That by two immutable things, in which it was impossible for God to lie, we might have a strong consolation, who have fled for refuge to lay hold upon the hope set before us:
My covenant will I not break, nor alter the thing that is gone out of my lips.
corruption_summary: God's faithfulness is treated as a general disposition, and Scripture grounds it in specific words He cannot take back.
corruption_paragraphs: John 10:35 is one of the most consequential parenthetical remarks in the Gospels. The Lord is under threat of stoning, He appeals to a single phrase in a psalm, and He interrupts His own argument to say and the scripture cannot be broken — not the passage, not the book, but the Scripture as such, and He does it while resting an argument on the force of one word. That is the highest possible view of the text, asserted casually, by the One with most authority to revise it.

The pastoral weight of the doctrine is in Psalm 89:34 and its wording is deliberately double: My covenant will I not break, nor alter the thing that is gone out of my lips. Not break, and not alter — because a promise quietly revised is broken more effectively than one repudiated outright. The believer's assurance rests on nothing about himself; it rests on the fact that specific sentences have gone out of God's lips and cannot be recalled. Hebrews 6 makes exactly this argument, saying God confirmed His promise with an oath — not for His own sake but so that we might have strong consolation from two immutable things.

The corresponding obligation is the one the Reformed have taken seriously in worship: what God has made inviolable, men may not adjust. Deuteronomy 4:2 forbids adding and diminishing, Revelation 22:18 repeats it at the canon's close, and the whole regulative instinct follows from taking the text as unbreakable rather than as raw material. A church that trims the hard sentences for a modern hearing has not made Scripture more accessible; it has treated as breakable what its Lord said could not be broken.
roots_summary: Greek luo (G3089), to loose, break; iota and keraia (G2503, G2762), jot and tittle; adunaton pseusasthai (G102, G5574), impossible to lie; Hebrew chalal (H2490), to profane, break.
roots_lines: Greek ou dunatai luthenai (G3089) — cannot be broken; John 10:35.
Greek iota / keraia (G2503, G2762) — the smallest letter and the smallest stroke; Matthew 5:18, Luke 16:17.
Hebrew chalal (H2490) — to profane, break; Psalm 89:31, 89:34, Numbers 30:2.
usage: “The scripture cannot be broken” — said in passing, while resting an argument on one word.
“Nor alter the thing that is gone out of my lips” — not break, and not alter.
“It was impossible for God to lie” — two immutable things, for strong consolation.

pos: n. pl. (the powers of the soul — understanding, will, affections, conscience, memory)
etymology: Latin facultas, capability, from facere, to do. The older divines analyse man by his faculties, and the doctrine of depravity is a statement about all of them at once.
biblical_def: The faculties are the soul's powers, and the great commandment addresses them together: “thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind, and with all thy strength” (Mar 12:30). Paul prays for the whole man: “I pray God your whole spirit and soul and body be preserved blameless” (1Th 5:23). They are trained by use: strong meat belongs to them “who by reason of use have their senses exercised to discern both good and evil” (Heb 5:14). The Fall darkened them: men have “the understanding darkened, being alienated from the life of God through the ignorance that is in them” (Eph 4:18). And renewal reaches them: “be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind” (Rom 12:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines faculty as any mental power or capacity; the powers of the mind, as the faculties of the soul, being the understanding, the will, the memory and the imagination.
webster_full: FACULTY, n. That power of the mind or intellect which enables it to receive, revive or modify perceptions; as the faculty of seeing, of hearing, of imagining.
The faculties of the mind are its powers or capacities, as the understanding, the will, the memory, the affections.
2. The power of doing any thing; ability.
3. Facility of performance; the peculiar skill derived from practice, or practice aided by nature.
scriptures: And thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind, and with all thy strength: this is the first commandment.
And the very God of peace sanctify you wholly; and I pray God your whole spirit and soul and body be preserved blameless unto the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ.
Heb 5:14
But strong meat belongeth to them that are of full age, even those who by reason of use have their senses exercised to discern both good and evil.
Eph 4:18
Having the understanding darkened, being alienated from the life of God through the ignorance that is in them, because of the blindness of their heart:
Rom 12:2
And be not conformed to this world: but be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind, that ye may prove what is that good, and acceptable, and perfect, will of God.
corruption_summary: One faculty is elevated and the rest neglected, and the great commandment names four in a row.
corruption_paragraphs: Every generation of the church has a favourite faculty and mistrusts the others. The rationalist wants the understanding and is suspicious of feeling; the revivalist wants the affections and is impatient with doctrine; the moralist wants the will and treats both as decoration. Mark 12:30 refuses the choice by listing heart, soul, mind and strength in one breath, and the effect of the piling up is that no part of a man is left out of the command. Jonathan Edwards's contribution was to show that the affections are not a lower faculty to be tolerated but the seat of what a man actually is, and that a doctrine held with no warmth has not been believed in the way Scripture means by believing.

The doctrine of depravity is a claim about all the faculties rather than a claim that any is destroyed. Ephesians 4:18 says the understanding is darkened, which presumes it still functions — fallen men reason, build, compose and legislate impressively. The will still chooses, and chooses freely according to its nature; the conscience still accuses and excuses. What is denied is that any faculty is neutral or unimpaired, which is why regeneration must be a work on the man himself and not merely the supply of better information to a sound instrument.

Hebrews 5:14 is the practical corrective to a passive view of all this: their senses are exercised by reason of use. Discernment is trained, like a palate or an ear, by repeated application to real cases, and it does not arrive with conversion. This is why a believer of thirty years may be no wiser than one of three — the years supply the opportunity and not the exercise — and why the ordinary means of grace are ordinary: Scripture read, preaching heard, sacraments taken, obedience attempted, week after week, until the faculties have been formed by them.
roots_summary: Greek kardia (G2588), heart; psuche (G5590), soul; dianoia (G1271), mind; aistheterion (G145), faculty of perception, sense.
roots_lines: Greek kardia…psuche…dianoia…ischus (G2588, G5590, G1271, G2479) — heart, soul, mind, strength; Mark 12:30, Luke 10:27.
Greek aistheterion (G145) — organ of perception, faculty; Hebrews 5:14 only.
Greek nous (G3563) — mind; Romans 12:2, Ephesians 4:23, 1 Corinthians 2:16.
usage: “Heart… soul… mind… strength” — four in a row, and none left out.
“The understanding darkened” — darkened, and still working.
“By reason of use have their senses exercised” — trained, not issued.

pos: n. (a written composition handling a subject in order; Luke's word for his own Gospel)
etymology: Old French traitis, from Latin tractare, to handle. The AV uses it once, and it is Luke describing the third Gospel to Theophilus (Act 1:1).
biblical_def: A treatise is an ordered written account. Luke opens Acts by naming his Gospel one: “The former treatise have I made, O Theophilus, of all that Jesus began both to do and teach” (Act 1:1). His preface describes the method — many had taken in hand to set forth in order a declaration, and he, “having had perfect understanding of all things from the very first, to write unto thee in order”, that Theophilus “mightest know the certainty of those things, wherein thou hast been instructed” (Luk 1:3–4). John states his own purpose: “these are written, that ye might believe that Jesus is the Christ” (John 20:31), and concedes the limit: “the world itself could not contain the books that should be written” (John 21:25). Paul, in prison, sends for “the books, but especially the parchments” (2Ti 4:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines treatise as a tract; a written composition on a particular subject, in which the principles of it are discussed or explained.
webster_full: TREATISE, n. A tract; a written composition on a particular subject, in which the principles of it are discussed or explained.
A treatise implies more form and method than an essay, but may be without the formality of a regular system.
scriptures: Act 1:1
The former treatise have I made, O Theophilus, of all that Jesus began both to do and teach,
Luk 1:3
It seemed good to me also, having had perfect understanding of all things from the very first, to write unto thee in order, most excellent Theophilus,
John 20:31
But these are written, that ye might believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God; and that believing ye might have life through his name.
John 21:25
And there are also many other things which Jesus did, the which, if they should be written every one, I suppose that even the world itself could not contain the books that should be written. Amen.
The cloke that I left at Troas with Carpus, when thou comest, bring with thee, and the books, but especially the parchments.
corruption_summary: Inspiration is imagined as dictation, and Luke describes research, sources and an editorial plan.
corruption_paragraphs: Luke's preface is the most valuable four verses in the New Testament on how Scripture came to be, and it describes ordinary historical labour. Many had taken in hand to set forth a declaration; eyewitnesses and ministers of the word had delivered them; Luke had perfect understanding of all things from the very first; and he determined to write in order. Research, sources, arrangement, an intended reader and a stated purpose — and the result is inspired Scripture. Inspiration in the Reformed account does not bypass the writer's mind, temperament, vocabulary or method; it governs the outcome, so that what Luke wrote by investigation is exactly what God said.

That is why the Gospels differ in arrangement without contradicting, why Luke reads like a physician and Mark like a man in a hurry, and why John states an editorial principle openly — many other signs truly did Jesus, which are not written in this book; but these are written, that ye might believe. A selection was made, on purpose, for an effect. Recognising this protects the text from two opposite errors: the reader who is scandalised to find design in it, and the reader who treats the design as evidence that the content is invented.

Second Timothy 4:13 is the small human detail that belongs beside all this. Paul is near the end, in a cold prison, and what he asks for is a cloak, the books, and especially the parchments. The man who wrote a third of the New Testament wanted something to read. That is a reasonable rebuke to any Christian who supposes that a spiritual man has outgrown study, and a fair description of what this dictionary is for: an ordered handling of words, so that what is already written may be better understood.
roots_summary: Greek logos (G3056), account, word, treatise; anatassomai (G392), to draw up in order; kathexes (G2517), in order, consecutively; membrana (G3200), parchment.
roots_lines: Greek proton logon (G3056) — the former treatise, the first account; Acts 1:1.
Greek kathexes (G2517) — in order, one after another; Luke 1:3, Acts 11:4, 18:23.
Greek biblia / membranas (G975, G3200) — the books, especially the parchments; 2 Timothy 4:13.
usage: “The former treatise have I made, O Theophilus” — Luke, of his own Gospel.
“To write unto thee in order” — research, sources, and a plan.
“The books, but especially the parchments” — asked for from a prison.
